title: Nickel Mines
hookLine: in 2006 an Amish community in Pennsylvania publicly forgave the man who shot their children, and comforted his family

cards: Nickel Mines is a small place in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, with farms, buggies and a one-room Amish schoolhouse.

One autumn morning, a man from the area, not Amish, walked into that school with guns and shot girls in their classroom, and then himself. This lesson won't linger on the details. What it remembers is what came next.
Within hours, Amish neighbors went to the gunman's family. Not to accuse. To comfort them.

teach.b: This account follows the book Amish Grace, written by scholars who studied the community's response. First, the visits.
The book describes Amish neighbors going to the gunman's widow and his parents in the first days, to say they held no grudge, and to sit with them.
Amish neighbors, it says, were among the mourners at his burial, standing with the family of the man who had done this. Second, the gifts.

Gifts of money came in for the Amish families, and the book tells how the community shared some of it with the gunman's widow and children, who had lost someone too and had done nothing wrong. Those are the other family.

teach.h: IF YE FORGIVE MEN THEIR TRESPASSES.
teach.b: The authors trace the response to the Lord's Prayer, which the book describes as prayed daily in Amish homes, and to Jesus's words right after it in Matthew: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you."
The same line these Christian voices began with. In the book's telling, that verse wasn't a nice idea. It was something you do, even here.
Fourth, what forgiveness didn't mean. The book is careful about this. The families grieved, deeply and for a long time.
Forgiving didn't erase the loss, or call what happened anything but evil.
It meant giving up the right to revenge, and refusing to let bitterness take over. Some outsiders praised it; some questioned whether it came too fast. The authors take both reactions seriously.
What's left is a plain picture: grieving parents sitting with a widow, remembering that the man who did this also left behind a family.

how: Amish Christians pray the Lord's Prayer and take its line about forgiving others as something to practice; in the book Amish Grace, Amish people interviewed describe forgiveness as giving up revenge, not forgetting the loss.

games.q: your community has just suffered something terrible, and the man who did it is dead. his widow and children live nearby. what does the Amish community do, in the book's account?
o: stay away from his family entirely.
go to his family to comfort them.
ask the town to move them away.
games.why: they went to his family within hours, to say they held no grudge, and later shared gifts with his widow and children.

practice: Think of someone who has caused harm, close to you or far off in the news, and turn instead to the people around them: a parent, a partner, a child, who didn't choose what happened and carry it anyway.
Picture one of them alone at a kitchen table, and let a small wish rise for them: some peace, some company, someone at the door. If you pray, you can hold that family in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Nickel Mines. The Amish community in Pennsylvania that, after a shooting at its school, went to comfort the gunman's family. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the other family. Grief stays, and revenge goes. Day nine hundred fifty-five, done.
